notes: Numeric answers are verified by tests/test_drills.py against training/daily_drills/drill_checks.py. Judgment drills carry a rubric; the simulator never declares a single correct trade for them. All scenario facts are hypothetical unless a source is cited.

drills.title: Cap-rate move, NOI constant
drills.question: The 10-year Treasury rises 20 bp. A property's NOI is unchanged. Required cap rates move from 6.0% to 6.5%. What is the percentage change in asset value?
drills.solution: V = NOI/c, so V1/V0 = c0/c1 = 6.0/6.5 = 0.92308. Change = -7.69%. Shortcut: dV/V is about -dc/c = -0.5/6.5, which is -7.7% here; for small moves use -dc/c0 = -8.3% as an upper bound on the loss.
common_mistakes: Computing -0.5/6.0 = -8.33% (uses the old cap in the denominator; that is the first-order approximation, not the exact answer)
Assuming value falls 20 bp-worth because Treasuries moved 20 bp: the cap moved 50 bp, so the spread to Treasuries widened 30 bp
drills.intuition: Value is inversely proportional to the cap rate. The cap-rate move was 2.5x the Treasury move, so risk premia, not just rates, repriced.
drills.takeaway: Ask why the cap moved more than the risk-free rate: credit availability, growth expectations, or risk appetite. Each has a different persistence.

drills.title: Room revenue and a three-point occupancy decline
drills.question: A hotel has 120 rooms, 72% occupancy and $125 ADR. Compute annual room revenue and the revenue lost if occupancy falls three points with ADR unchanged.
drills.solution: Available room-nights = 120 x 365 = 43,800. Rooms sold = 43,800 x 0.72 = 31,536. Revenue = 31,536 x $125 = $3,942,000. RevPAR = 0.72 x 125 = $90.00. Three points = 0.03 x 43,800 = 1,314 room-nights x $125 = $164,250 (4.17% of revenue).
common_mistakes: Treating a 3-point decline as 3% of revenue (it is 3/72 = 4.17%)
Forgetting the x365 annualization
drills.intuition: Occupancy points scale with available room-nights; a 'point' is 438 room-nights per year for a 120-room hotel.
drills.takeaway: At roughly 65-75% flow-through on lost rooms revenue for a limited-service hotel, about $107k-$123k of NOI is lost, which is $1.2m-$1.4m of value at a 9% cap. Small operating moves have large value effects.

drills.title: Strong payrolls, falling yields
drills.question: A monthly employment report beats consensus, yet Treasury yields fall on the day. Give three plausible explanations and the data you would check for each.

rubric: Revisions: prior months revised down so the level of employment is weaker than thought (check the revision lines)
Composition: headline beat but wages, hours or the household survey/unemployment rate were weak (check average hourly earnings, hours, unemployment rate)
Positioning: market was positioned for an even stronger number or short duration; 'buy the fact' short covering (check prior-day moves, CFTC positioning, consensus whisper)
Other news the same day dominated (geopolitics, a Fed speaker, auction results, risk-off in equities)
Explicitly does not claim one explanation is certain; names a test for each

drills.solution: The release is a bundle: headline, revisions, wages, hours, the household survey. Prices react to the surprise in the bundle relative to what was positioned, not to the headline relative to consensus. Strong answers name at least three of: revisions, wage weakness, unemployment-rate rise, positioning, competing news, and say what data would discriminate between them.
common_mistakes: Calling the market 'irrational'
Giving explanations with no way to check them
drills.intuition: Expected information is priced; only surprise moves prices, and surprise is measured against positioning as well as consensus.
drills.takeaway: Before trading a release, write down which components matter and what is already priced.

drills.title: Equal IRRs, different leverage
drills.question: Two acquisitions show the same 15% projected levered IRR. One uses 80% leverage, the other 40%. Explain why the investments are not equivalent.

rubric: Same IRR at higher leverage implies a lower unlevered return on the 80% LTV deal; the asset itself is weaker
Equity volatility scales with 1/(1-LTV): 5x asset volatility at 80% vs 1.67x at 40%
Survival: at 80% LTV a 20% value decline eliminates equity; at 40% it takes 60%
Refinancing/maturity and covenant risk (DSCR, cash traps) are much larger at 80%
The 15% is a point estimate; the distribution and the downside differ; risk-adjusted they are not comparable

drills.solution: Unlevered return r_A solves r_E = r_A + (L/(1-L))(r_A - r_D). With r_D = 7%: at 40% LTV r_A = 0.6 x 15% + 0.4 x 7% = 11.8%; at 80% r_A = 0.2 x 15% + 0.8 x 7% = 8.6%. The 80% deal is a lower-quality asset dressed in leverage, with 5x equity volatility multiplier and a 20% value cushion.
common_mistakes: Treating IRR as a sufficient statistic
Ignoring that leverage changes the probability of losing control of the asset
drills.intuition: Leverage manufactures return from spread and manufactures fragility from volatility.
drills.takeaway: Compare deals on unlevered returns and downside equity outcomes, then choose leverage deliberately.

drills.title: RevPAR up, NOI down
drills.question: A hotel reports RevPAR up 4% year over year but NOI down 6%. Identify at least four mechanisms that could explain it.

rubric: Labor cost inflation (wage rates, overtime, contract labor) growing faster than revenue
RevPAR growth from occupancy rather than ADR raises variable costs per occupied room (housekeeping, laundry, supplies, commissions)
Channel mix shift to OTAs raises commissions; loyalty/brand fee increases
Insurance and property tax increases (fixed charges below GOP)
Loss of other revenue (F&B, parking, meeting) so TRevPAR growth < RevPAR growth
Utilities, repairs, or one-time items; reserve or management fee changes

drills.solution: RevPAR is a top-line rooms metric. NOI depends on TRevPAR, cost per occupied room, undistributed expenses, fees, and fixed charges. Occupancy-driven RevPAR growth has lower flow-through than ADR-driven growth because each occupied room carries variable cost.
common_mistakes: Assuming RevPAR growth implies margin growth
Ignoring below-GOP fixed charges
drills.intuition: Hotels have high operating leverage in both directions, and cost inflation can overwhelm modest revenue growth.
drills.takeaway: Underwrite flow-through, not RevPAR; decompose RevPAR growth into occupancy and ADR.

drills.title: NOI decline plus cap expansion under different leverage
drills.question: A property is worth $10 million at a 7% cap. NOI falls 12% and cap rates widen to 8%. Compute the new value and the equity change at 50%, 65% and 75% LTV (debt unchanged).
common_mistakes: Adding -12% and -12.5% to get -24.5% instead of multiplying (0.88 x 7/8 = 0.77)
Forgetting the debt does not shrink
drills.intuition: Income and multiple shocks compound multiplicatively, then leverage multiplies again.
drills.takeaway: At 75% LTV this property needs a refinance with fresh equity; a 1.25x DSCR covenant is likely breached too. Survival, not return, becomes the question.

drills.title: Recovering from a drawdown
drills.question: A portfolio falls 35%. What gain is required to return to the prior peak?
common_mistakes: Answering 35%
drills.intuition: Losses are taken on a larger base than the subsequent gains.
drills.takeaway: Avoiding large drawdowns is worth more than capturing the last increment of upside.

drills.title: Debt-yield constraint
drills.question: A lender requires a minimum 9.5% debt yield. Underwritten NOI is $1.2 million. What is the maximum loan under this test?
common_mistakes: Multiplying instead of dividing
drills.intuition: Debt yield is the lender's unlevered return if it takes the property at the loan amount; it ignores rate and amortization.
drills.takeaway: Debt yield binds when rates are low or cap rates compressed; it protects lenders against inflated values.

drills.title: Loan constant and DSCR
drills.question: A $10 million loan at 7% on a 30-year monthly amortization. NOI is $1.0 million. Compute the annual loan constant and the DSCR.
common_mistakes: Using the interest rate (7%) as the constant
Using annual instead of monthly compounding
drills.intuition: The constant exceeds the rate because it includes principal repayment.
drills.takeaway: When the constant exceeds the cap rate, leverage reduces current cash yield.

drills.title: Break-even probability and abstention
drills.question: A distressed-asset bid gains $1.5m if the tenant renews and loses $4.5m if it leaves. Your estimate of the probability of non-renewal is 20-35%. Compute the break-even probability and decide: bid, pass, or gather information.

rubric: Computes p* = G/(G+L) = 25%
Recognizes the estimate range straddles p*, so EV sign is unknown
Recommends gathering information (tenant conversations, space-planning activity, broker intelligence) or restructuring (lower price, tenant-contingent earn-out) before bidding
Notes that abstention is a legitimate outcome if information cannot be obtained

drills.solution: p* = 1.5/(1.5 + 4.5) = 25%. EV at 20% = 0.8(1.5) - 0.2(4.5) = +$0.30m; at 35% = 0.65(1.5) - 0.35(4.5) = -$0.60m. The decision depends on a number you do not know; buy information or change the payoff.
common_mistakes: Using the midpoint (27.5%) as if it were known and bidding or passing confidently
drills.intuition: Break-even analysis tells you whether your ignorance matters.
drills.takeaway: When the range straddles break-even, the correct action is usually to reduce uncertainty or reshape the payoff, not to guess.

drills.title: E-mini S&P 500 P&L
drills.question: You are long 3 E-mini S&P 500 futures ($50 x index) at 5,000.00 and exit at 4,940.00. Compute the P&L and the notional exposure at entry.
common_mistakes: Using the $250 multiplier of the legacy full-size contract
Measuring loss against margin posted rather than notional
drills.intuition: Futures P&L follows notional, not margin; margin is a performance bond, not the investment.
drills.takeaway: Size futures on notional and volatility, never on margin.

drills.title: EUR/USD P&L
drills.question: You are long EUR 2,000,000 against USD at EUR/USD 1.0850 and close at 1.0720. What is the P&L and in what currency?
common_mistakes: Reporting the P&L in EUR
Inverting the quote
drills.intuition: A BASE/QUOTE position earns in QUOTE currency per unit of BASE.
drills.takeaway: Always state the pair direction and the P&L currency before computing.

drills.title: Duration price change
drills.question: A bond priced at 98.00 has modified duration 8.0. Yields rise 25 bp. Estimate the price change in points and percent (first order).
drills.solution: dP/P = -D x dy = -8.0 x 0.0025 = -2.0%; dP = -2.0% x 98 = -1.96 points. Convexity would make the actual decline slightly smaller.
common_mistakes: Using dy = 25 or 0.25 instead of 0.0025
drills.intuition: Duration is the percentage price sensitivity per unit of yield.
drills.takeaway: Express yield changes as decimals in every duration formula.

drills.title: Conflicting hotel signals
drills.question: In your market, hotel occupancy growth is strong, but lenders are cutting loan proceeds, credit spreads are widening and Treasury yields are rising. Should hotel values rise or fall over the next 12 months? Explain why the answer is not mechanically determined, and state what you would do with a pending acquisition.

rubric: Separates the cash-flow channel (occupancy -> NOI, which raises value) from the discount-rate and financing channels (rates, spreads, proceeds, which lower value)
Notes that the net effect depends on relative magnitudes and persistence; quantifies with an example (e.g., NOI +5% vs cap +75 bp)
Recognizes that reduced proceeds shrink the buyer pool and raise required equity returns, which affects transaction prices before appraisals
Asks whether occupancy growth is ADR-led or occupancy-led and what flow-through is, and whether supply is coming
Recommends a conditional action (re-price the bid on lower leverage, negotiate a financing contingency, or wait) and states what data would change it
Treats 'wait' or 'pass' as legitimate if the financing cannot be secured

drills.solution: Example: NOI +5% and cap 9.0% -> 9.75% gives value x 1.05 x 9/9.75 = 0.969 (-3.1%). With NOI +10% and the same cap move, value is +1.5%. The answer depends on magnitudes. Lower proceeds also mean fewer buyers can close, which pushes transaction prices down before fundamentals change. A disciplined buyer re-underwrites at 55% LTV, requires the return to work at that leverage, and is prepared to wait.
common_mistakes: Answering 'up because occupancy is strong' or 'down because rates rose' without weighing both
Ignoring the financing channel
drills.intuition: Private CRE prices are set by marginal buyers who need financing; capital availability can dominate fundamentals over 6-18 months.
drills.takeaway: Map each signal to a valuation channel, quantify, and decide on conditions rather than forecasts.

drills.title: Loaded cap rate and reassessment
drills.question: NOI before property tax is $900,000. The market cap rate is 8%. After a sale, property tax will be 2.0% of the purchase price. The seller's current tax bill is $60,000. Compute (a) value with reassessment and (b) the overstatement if you capitalize NOI using the seller's tax bill.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the seller's NOI
Applying the tax to the old assessed value
drills.intuition: When tax depends on price, value and tax must be solved together.
drills.takeaway: In reassessment jurisdictions, always underwrite tax on your own basis.
